Union-rescored and temperature-calibrated fusion, as well as direct adaptations of prior query-refinement methods, are needed.

The efficiency evidence is limited to these benchmark corpora and lacks important protocol details such as the indexing backend, exact versus approximate search, precision, warmup, batching, and latency variance. Storage calculations cover embeddings but omit resident model memory, textual/OCR artifacts, and index overhead, so the broader deployment claims are only partially supported.

The optimized query vectors are apparently unconstrained; the paper does not study whether their norms change or whether they leave the normalized representation manifold. Details such as gradient flow through the consensus target are also insufficiently explicit. These omissions weaken both the geometric interpretation and reproducibility.

Generality is demonstrated only within the ViDoRe benchmark family. ViDoRe 1 is saturated, ViDoRe 3 evaluates only two primary models and uses official markdown rather than the earlier OCR pipeline, and the strongest primary model is excluded there. Claims of architecture-agnostic, real-world scalability would benefit from another retrieval domain and a genuinely large corpus.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-cikag5ex/call-6c235bbda4e441a58cbc4ae5ecb9271e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a practical problem with a simple, clearly formulated, retraining-free method applicable to both single- and multi-vector primary retrievers.

The evaluation is broad: three ViDoRe benchmark generations, multiple vision/text model pairings, tuned and zero-shot settings, NDCG and recall, and comparisons with rank fusion, score fusion, and a multimodal reranker.
The zero-shot ViDoRe 3 results provide useful evidence that the method's gains are not entirely caused by per-dataset tuning.

The paper includes valuable ablations of learning rate and optimization steps, candidate-pool construction, loss choice, extra search, and primary/complementary role assignment, together with latency and index-storage measurements.
weaknesses: The central empirical advantage over tuned score fusion is too small to establish convincingly: average ViDoRe 2 NDCG@5 is 62.3 for GQR versus 62.1 for tuned min-max fusion, while the corresponding ViDoRe 3 relative gains are 2.89% versus 2.66%. No paired significance tests, confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, or query-level variance are reported, so these differences may be noise.

The latency and storage Pareto claims omit the strongest score-fusion systems from the Pareto plots. Those systems use the same two encoders and indexes but avoid GQR's iterative gradient steps, making them essential efficiency baselines given their nearly identical quality.

The resource accounting is incomplete. Reported memory is essentially raw per-document embedding storage and excludes model weights, index overhead, OCR text, and runtime memory. Calling the complementary retrievers lightweight is questionable when they contain roughly 4–7B parameters; total system memory could exceed that of the comparison model.

Novelty is moderate: prior work already optimizes query embeddings at inference using relevance feedback, and the principal change is replacing a cross-encoder teacher with another bi-encoder in a multimodal setting. Moreover, the auxiliary representation is never combined directly; it contributes only scalar scores, making the representation-level framing stronger than the demonstrated mechanism warrants.

The tuning protocol risks overfitting. GQR tunes two hyperparameters separately for every model pair and subset on a 10% split, whereas fusion weights use a coarse 0.1 grid and no temperature calibration. The paper does not clearly state whether development queries are excluded from reported results, provide split identifiers or sample counts, or quantify sensitivity to the small development sets.

Several claims are overstated. GQR averages a slight decrease on ViDoRe 1, harms some ViDoRe 2 subsets, and has negative cells on ViDoRe 3, contradicting unqualified claims of consistent improvement. The text also inconsistently reports the second storage advantage as approximately 24x versus 28x.

Reproducibility and scope remain limited: the promised code has no supplied link, important timing details such as index size, warm-up, batching, and variability are missing, and all quality evaluations belong to the closely related ViDoRe benchmark family rather than an independent large-scale retrieval setting.

The empirical study is unusually broad for this problem: three ViDoRe benchmarks, multiple vision/text retriever pairs, tuned and zero-shot settings, rank- and score-fusion baselines, reranker comparisons, two metrics, and several design ablations.

GQR produces consistent aggregate improvements. Particularly useful is the zero-shot ViDoRe 3 result, where one configuration improves all six model-pair averages and has lower cross-pair variability than the fusion baselines.

The efficiency results are compelling: Colnomic+Linq nearly matches Llama-Nemo while reporting roughly 14x lower query latency and over 50x lower embedding storage, while Colnomic+Jina slightly surpasses it at substantially lower cost.

The paper is well organized and supplies an algorithm, hyperparameter tables, per-subset results, latency breakdowns, and analyses of candidate pools, objectives, role reversal, and optimization dynamics.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. GQR closely follows prior test-time query-representation optimization, primarily replacing cross-encoder feedback with another bi-encoder and introducing a consensus target. A controlled comparison with prior query-refinement algorithms under identical candidates and budgets is missing; moreover, the KL-target and Jensen-Shannon variants in Table 18 perform about as well as the proposed consensus loss.

The claimed advantage over strong score fusion is small and lacks uncertainty analysis: on ViDoRe 2, GQR averages 62.3 versus 62.1 for tuned min-max fusion; on ViDoRe 3, the relative gains are 2.89% versus 2.66%. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, query counts, or resampling analyses. GQR also searches 18 learning-rate/step combinations per subset, versus nine weights for fusion, creating a possible tuning-selection advantage.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including whether gradients are stopped through the consensus distribution, whether raw-score softmaxes use temperature calibration, optimizer initialization/state, numerical precision, and the retrieval/index backend. The manuscript says code is released but provides no code URL. These omissions matter because heterogeneous retrievers can have very different score scales and entropies.

The broad efficiency claims should be qualified. Storage calculations cover embedding payloads but omit model weights, ANN/index overhead, OCR-derived text, and the cost of serving two multi-billion-parameter encoders. Latency is measured only on one A100 without error bars or sufficiently detailed warm-up, batching, index-size, and search-protocol information.

The reranker comparison is not fully controlled: GQR uses the union of two retrievers' top-10 lists, whereas the reranker appears to receive candidates from only the primary retriever. Consequently, both candidate recall and candidate count differ.

Some statements overclaim the tables: ViDoRe 3 contains small per-subset degradations, despite the claim of improvement across every pair and subset, and several ViDoRe 1 pair averages decline slightly. Evaluation is also confined to the ViDoRe family, leaving the claimed architecture/task generality and robustness to severely miscalibrated complementary retrievers insufficiently established.
